title: Isomorphic Strings
statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, determine if they are isomorphic.

Two strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic if the characters in `s` can be replaced to get `t`.

All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. No two characters may map to the same character, but a character may map to itself.
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII characters.

examples.explanation: e maps to a, g maps to d. Thus the mapping is valid.
o cannot map to both a and r.

editorial.approach: Create two map dictionaries. One maps s[i] to t[i] and the other maps t[i] to s[i]. Iterate character-by-character: if a mapping mismatch occurs, return false, else insert mappings. If loop completes, return true.
editorial.complexity: O(n) time / O(1) space (since ASCII set is small, 256)

hints: You need a one-to-one character mapping: `s[i] <-> t[i]`.
Use two hash maps (or arrays): one to track mapping from `s` to `t` and another from `t` to `s`.
Iterate through the indices. If `s[i]` is already mapped to a character other than `t[i]`, or `t[i]` is mapped to a character other than `s[i]`, return false.

bruteForceSolution.explanation: Convert both strings to their first-occurrence index sequence representation, then check if they are identical.

optimizedSolution.explanation: Use two arrays or hash maps to record character mappings. Ensure bidirectional consistency in O(n) time.
optimizedSolution.spaceComplexity: O(1) (since ASCII dictionary size is constant, 256)

interviewExplanation: A brute-force indexing sequence takes O(n^2) time due to `.indexOf`. We optimize to O(n) using bidirectional hash tables mapping `s[i] -> t[i]` and `t[i] -> s[i]`. Auxiliary space is O(1) as the printable ASCII character set size is small and fixed.
